summary: This unit teaches you to work in ways that protect Jamaica's water, energy, land, reefs and beaches. You will learn to save water and electricity, sort and reduce waste, handle chemicals and hazardous waste safely, protect coral reefs, beaches and turtles, buy local, measure and record resource use, and report problems. You will also learn how to encourage guests and co-workers to take part, in a friendly and polite way.

blocks.p: Tourism is one of Jamaica's biggest earners, and guests come for our beaches, reefs, rivers, hills and food. If we waste water, burn too much electricity, pollute the sea or damage the reef, we harm the very things that visitors come to see and that Jamaicans live on. Working in an **environmentally sustainable** way means using water, energy and materials so that less is wasted, and looking after the natural places around us so that they last. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Sustainable habits are usually simple: switch off, fix the leak, sort the rubbish, keep the chemicals in their place and tell your supervisor. They also **save money** for the villa, and good villas are proud of them.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practical tasks you walk through a mock villa to find resource waste, write maintenance reports, read a meter, write an action plan, set up a waste separation station and make a guest green-tips card. The assessor looks at your safe actions, your reports and your explanations.

sections.title: Why sustainability matters, and the rules

head: Reason
What it means for a villa
rows: Cost
Wasted water, electricity and food are wasted money. Savings help the villa pay wages and stay open
Guests
Many guests choose properties that care for the environment, and notice litter, dirty water and wasteful habits
Jamaica's natural resources
Water supplies are limited, especially in dry spells and droughts. Power is costly. The reefs, beaches, mangroves and forests protect the land, feed the people and bring the visitors

head: Step
Meaning
Example in a villa
rows: Reduce
Use or buy less in the first place. This is the best step
Refillable water jugs instead of many small plastic bottles
Reuse
Use the same thing again
Reuse glass jars for storage; reuse towels when the guest asks
Recycle
Turn waste into new products
Sorted glass, cans, paper and plastic bottles

blocks.note: **Reduce comes first.** Recycling needs energy and effort, and not every item can be recycled in Jamaica. The best waste is the waste that is never made.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Body or rule
What it does
rows: NEPA (National Environment and Planning Agency)
Looks after the environment and planning, permits and protected areas, including reefs, wildlife and beaches
NSWMA (National Solid Waste Management Authority)
Collects and manages solid waste (garbage) across the island
NWC (National Water Commission)
Supplies water and may ask customers to save water during droughts
The Ministry and agencies for fisheries
Set closed seasons and legal sizes for fish, lobster and conch
Single-use plastics rules

Jamaica has banned certain single-use plastic items, including some plastic bags, plastic drinking straws and foam (expanded polystyrene) food containers. Lists are updated from time to time, so ask your supervisor for the current rules

blocks.note: Jamaica's climate and geography make us careful about water. Many parishes have dry spells and droughts, and many villas keep water in tanks. Tourism depends on a healthy environment, so what we do at work has a real effect on the island.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Do your own tasks in a sustainable way, every day.
Notice waste and problems and **report them**.
Follow the villa's rules for water, energy, waste and chemicals.
Set a good example. Guests and co-workers copy what they see.

blocks.p: Water is precious. A dripping tap or a running toilet wastes many litres every day, and the villa pays for all of it. In a dry spell, wasted water may mean that guests have none.

head: Where
What to do
rows: Guest rooms and bathrooms
Check taps, showers and toilets for drips and leaks and **report them at once**
Follow the towel and linen reuse card: change towels and sheets only when the guest asks or on the set day
Do not run taps while cleaning; use a bucket or a filled basin
Kitchen
Wash fruit and vegetables and dishes in a filled sink or basin, not under a running tap
Run the dishwasher only when it is full
Defrost food in the fridge, not under running water
Laundry
Wash full loads
Use the right water level and the cycle that suits the load
Check hoses and valves for leaks
Outside
Sweep patios and paths instead of hosing them
Water the garden early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when less water evaporates, and at the roots, not over the leaves
Use rainwater from the tank on the garden
Mulch beds to keep the soil moist
Pool
Use a cover to cut evaporation
Check for leaks; do not top up more than needed

head: Item
What it does
rows: Tap aerator
A small part screwed onto the end of a tap that mixes air into the water and cuts the flow
Low-flow shower head
Uses less water each minute and still gives a good spray
Dual-flush toilet
Gives a small flush for liquid and a larger one for solid waste
Rainwater tank
Stores rainwater from the roof for the garden and cleaning

blocks.note: Rainwater from a roof tank is **not** treated drinking water unless the villa has treated and tested it. Use it for the garden and cleaning, not for drinking, unless your supervisor says it has been treated to drinking standard.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Greywater** is used water from sinks, showers and washing machines (not toilets). After proper treatment, it can be reused on a garden. Water that has had a lot of bleach, strong cleaners or food oil in it must not go on plants. Follow the villa's system and rules.

ul: Use water only where it is needed.
Report every leak quickly.
Share the guest information card about conserving water.
Know how much water is in the tank and where the valves and pump switch are.

blocks.note: A small leak is easy to fix. A large one floods floors and wastes tank water. When you see a dripping tap or a running toilet, write down the room and the problem and tell the supervisor, or fill in the maintenance report, the same day.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Electricity is expensive in Jamaica, and most of it comes from burning imported fuel. Every unit you save is money saved and less pollution. Electricity is counted in **kilowatt hours (kWh)**: a 1 kW appliance running for one hour uses 1 kWh.

blocks.h: Where energy goes in a villa

head: Use
Ways to save
rows: Cooling (air conditioning and fans)
Switch off the AC, fans and lights in empty rooms, or set them as the villa's policy says
Keep doors and windows **closed** when the AC is on
Draw curtains in the hottest part of the day to keep the sun out
Set the AC to a moderate temperature, not the coldest
Clean the filters as maintenance asks
Use the breeze and ceiling fans where the weather allows
Lighting
Use **LED bulbs**: they use far less electricity for the same light and last longer
Use daylight
Use timers or motion sensors for outdoor lights
Hot water
Solar water heaters use heat from the sun, a free energy source, and are common in Jamaica
Do not leave hot taps running
Laundry
Wash full loads
Dry linen on a clothes line in the sun and breeze when weather allows
Kitchen and cold storage
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed; report a torn door seal, which lets cold air out and wastes power
Do not put hot food straight in the fridge
Switch off cooking equipment when not in use
Electronics
Switch off TVs, chargers and other items at the wall when not in use. Many use power even on standby

blocks.p: Energy used (kWh) = power (kW) × hours. Power in watts ÷ 1 000 gives kW.

head: Example
Working
Answer
rows: A 60 W bulb is on for 5 hours
0.3 kWh
Replace it with a 9 W LED: energy used for the same 5 hours
Saving per bulb per day
10 bulbs for 30 days
76.5 kWh

blocks.note: Your bill is for the units you use, plus other charges. Saving units cuts the bill. Ask your supervisor what the villa pays per unit, so that you can see what a saving is worth in J$.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Solar **photovoltaic (PV)** panels make electricity from sunlight, while a solar water heater uses the sun to heat water directly. Both reduce the power bought from the grid. Staff do not install or repair them: report any damage or fault.

blocks.h: If the guests are in the room

blocks.p: Follow the guests' wishes and keep them comfortable. Energy saving must never make guests unhappy or unsafe. Explain the energy card politely and let them choose.

blocks.note: Use the breeze: in many parts of Jamaica, opening windows in the evening and using fans keeps rooms comfortable at a fraction of the cost of air conditioning. Close windows again before turning the AC on.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Waste: reduce, sort, compost and dispose

blocks.p: **Waste separation** means sorting waste into groups at the place where it is made, so that each group can be recycled, composted or disposed of properly.

flow: Agree the groups with the collector and recyclers
Give each group a labelled bin, with words and a picture
Place bins where the waste is made: kitchen, pantry, pool area
Show staff what goes where
Empty and wash bins often
Check for wrong items and correct them

head: Group
What goes in
Notes
rows: Plastic bottles
Empty, rinsed drink bottles
Remove lids if the recycler asks; do not put in oily containers
Glass
Empty, rinsed bottles and jars
Never mix with broken window glass or ceramics; handle broken glass with care
Cans
Empty, rinsed aluminium and steel cans
Flatten if allowed
Paper and cardboard
Clean paper, boxes
Greasy or food-soiled paper and cardboard cannot be recycled: put in general waste
Food and garden waste
Fruit and vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, tea leaves, leaves and grass
Compost it. Avoid cooked meat, fish, bones and oil, which attract pests
General waste
Used tissues, dirty wrappers, items that cannot be recycled
The last choice
Hazardous waste
Batteries, fluorescent tubes, old paint, chemical containers, used oil
Keep apart in a closed, labelled box; see below

blocks.note: Rinse containers before putting them in the recycling. A dirty container can spoil a whole load of recycling and attracts flies and rats.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Compost** is rotted food and garden waste that is dug into the soil to feed plants. Put peelings and leaves in a heap or bin, mix in dry leaves, keep it moist but not soggy and turn it from time to time. After some weeks it becomes dark, crumbly and earthy. It saves waste, saves money on fertiliser and makes the garden healthier.
Hazardous waste can harm people, soil and the sea. It never goes in the general bin, is never burned or buried and is never poured into drains, gullies or the sea.

head: Item
How to handle it
rows: Used batteries
Tape the ends; keep in a closed box; send to a collector the supervisor has approved
Fluorescent tubes and energy-saving bulbs
Contain mercury. Keep whole in a box so they do not break
Used cooking oil
Leave it to cool; pour into a sealed container; arrange proper collection. Never pour down the drain
Chemical containers
Keep their labels and lids; never reuse for food or drinks
Old paint
Keep the lid on; store dry and locked
Wet wipes and kitchen grease
Do not flush or pour them down the drain. They block pipes and stop septic tanks working

blocks.note: Burning rubbish in the yard is harmful: the smoke damages people's health, pollutes the air and can start a bush fire. Always use the proper waste routes.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Buy only what you need, and in larger or refillable packs.
Use refillable jugs and dispensers instead of small plastic bottles and sachets.
Use cloth bags and reusable items instead of single-use plastic.
Plan food orders and portions to cut food waste (first in, first out).
Offer leftover food to staff or a charity where food safety rules allow, and never serve it again to guests.

blocks.note: Jamaica's rules on single-use plastics mean that villas should replace plastic straws and foam containers with paper, cardboard or reusable items. Ask your supervisor for the current list.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The chemicals you use to clean can harm people and the environment if they are misused. Used correctly, they do the job with less waste and less harm.

head: Do
Because
rows: Measure and dilute as the label says
Too strong wastes product and harms surfaces, skin and waterways; too weak does not clean
Use the right product for the job; use less when it will do
Saves money and reduces pollution
Use cloths and reusable mops where possible
Reduces single-use waste
Keep products in original labelled containers
Prevents mistakes and keeps the safety information
Read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS) to find out how to get rid of a chemical safely
Each product has its own rules
Choose products that are **biodegradable** when the villa can: they break down naturally and safely in soil or water
Less harm to waterways

flow: Keep people away
Check the label and the SDS
Wear the PPE the SDS says
Stop the spill reaching drains, gullies or the sea; use absorbent material
Clean up as the SDS says and dispose of the waste correctly
Report the spill

blocks.note: A spill of **pool chemical** near a drain is an emergency. Keep people away and follow the SDS and the villa's spill steps. Do not wash it into the drain with water unless the SDS says it is safe.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many villas outside the towns use a septic tank to treat sewage. Wet wipes, kitchen grease, oil, tampons, strong chemicals and large amounts of bleach can block pipes or kill the helpful bacteria in the tank, so it stops working and may overflow. Only human waste and toilet paper go down the toilet.

blocks.note: Septic tank overflow pollutes groundwater, rivers and the sea. A tank that smells or a toilet that drains slowly is a problem to report at once.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Reefs, beaches, wildlife and local suppliers

blocks.p: Coral reefs are built by tiny living animals and take many years to grow. They break the waves so that beaches are not washed away, they are home to the fish that fishers catch and that guests come to see, and they bring snorkellers and divers who spend money in the community. A damaged reef hurts the whole island.

head: Ecosystem
Why it matters
rows: Coral reef
Protects the coast; home to fish; draws visitors
Seagrass beds
Shelter young fish and feed turtles and other animals
Mangroves
Trees growing with roots in salty water; protect the shore from storms and shelter young fish
Beach and dunes
Home to nesting turtles and birds; protect the land from waves

blocks.h: What to tell guests going to the reef

ul: **Look, but do not touch**. Do not stand on, hold or break coral, and keep fins away from it.
Do not feed the fish, and do not take coral, shells, starfish or sand home.

Use a **reef-friendly sunscreen** and put it on well before going into the sea, and wear a rash guard or T-shirt. Look for mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) free of oxybenzone and octinoxate. 'Reef-safe' on a label is not regulated, so check the ingredients.
Choose licensed tour operators who tie up to a **mooring buoy** (a floating marker fixed near a reef) instead of dropping an anchor on the coral.
Bring all rubbish back from the boat and the beach.

blocks.note: Reef groups also ask visitors not to catch or eat **parrotfish**. These brightly coloured fish eat the algae (seaweed) that would otherwise smother the coral. Also, a **fish sanctuary** is a protected area of sea where fishing is not allowed, so that fish can grow and breed. Staff can tell guests about the sanctuaries.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Walk the beach each morning, wearing gloves, to collect plastic, bottles and fishing line, and sort them into the correct bins.
Put covered bins near the beach, so that rubbish does not blow into the sea.

Sea turtles nest on some Jamaican beaches in the nesting season. Do not rake, dig or drive over places where turtles may nest. Report tracks or nests to the supervisor, who contacts the right authority.
At night, **switch off, shade or point down any lights that face the beach**. Bright lights confuse baby turtles, which crawl towards the lights instead of the sea.
Put sun loungers, kayaks and other items away at night so that they do not block nesting turtles.
Do not leave food, plastic or cigarette ends on the sand.

head: Benefit
Explanation
rows: Fresher
Picked or caught close by
Fewer food miles
The distance food travels from where it is grown to the plate is shorter, so less fuel and less packaging are used
Supports the community
Money stays in Jamaica and supports farmers, fishers and makers
Real Jamaican taste
Ackee, callaloo, local fruit, fresh fish, coffee and rum cake are loved by guests

blocks.p: When buying local, still check **quality, freshness and cleanliness**, that the supplier is reliable and gives receipts, and that fish, lobster and conch are not bought in the **closed season** or below the legal size. Keep a list of approved local suppliers. Locally made items such as coffee, jams, crafts and rum cake make good welcome baskets.

blocks.note: Closed seasons protect fish and lobster while they breed. The authorities set the dates and legal sizes, which can change, so ask your supervisor and buy only from licensed suppliers who follow them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: On the same day and at about the same time each week, read the water and electricity meters
Write the readings on the record sheet with the date and your name
Subtract last week's reading from this week's: this is the amount used
Note how many guests stayed
Compare weeks and check against the bills
Report any reading that looks wrong

head: Meter
Reads in
Example
rows: Electricity
kWh
Last week 18 420 kWh; this week 18 605 kWh: used 185 kWh
Water
cubic metres (m³)
Last week 312 m³; this week 330 m³: used 18 m³ = 18 000 litres

blocks.p: A sudden rise while the villa is empty may show a **leak** (for example a toilet that keeps running) or equipment left on. Records show whether changes such as LED bulbs have worked, help set targets and plan repairs.
Report a dripping tap, a running toilet, a faulty air conditioner, an overflowing bin, a spill or a light left on. Small problems grow into big waste or harm.

flow: Make the area safe if that is part of your role, for example with a wet floor sign
Tell the supervisor or fill in the maintenance report
Give the place, what the problem is, the time and your name
Do not try repairs you are not trained for
Check later that it was fixed

head: Who
How
rows: Guests
A short, friendly card in each room explaining the towel reuse, asking them to switch off the AC when they go out and giving reef-care tips
Mention the points politely on arrival, without forcing anyone
Make it easy: refillable water jugs, reusable beach bags, clearly labelled bins
Co-workers
Lead by example
Explain the reason in team meetings and show the meter records
Thank staff when use goes down
Welcome and try good ideas from staff

blocks.note: People join in more willingly when they understand the reason. 'Please reuse your towel to help protect Jamaica's water' works better than a rule on its own.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: A housekeeper who has an idea to cut waste should tell her supervisor, with the cost and benefit of the idea. Writing it down with a simple estimate makes it easy for the manager to say yes.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: A dry spell at a Treasure Beach villa
c1.text: It has not rained for weeks and the water tank at a villa in Treasure Beach is low. Housekeeper Tonya notices that the toilet in Villa 2 keeps running after it has been flushed. In the kitchen, a helper washes a big bowl of vegetables under a running tap. In the garden, the gardener plans to water the plants at midday with the hose. A guest in Villa 3 has left a card on the bed that asks about the towel reuse programme.

c2.title: Cooling and lighting at a Negril villa
c2.text: A villa in Negril has sunny rooms that face west, and the air conditioning is used from noon. Housekeeper Marcia finds the curtains in an empty room wide open, the TV on standby and the charger plugged in. The villa is changing ten 60 W bulbs in the corridor to 9 W LED bulbs. These lights are on for 5 hours each day.

c3.title: After a beach party in Ocho Rios
c3.text: After a beach party at a villa in Ocho Rios, the staff have a lot of waste to sort. There are rinsed aluminium cans, a greasy pizza box, a pile of mango peelings and coffee grounds, and a broken fluorescent tube from the terrace. The villa has bins for plastic bottles, glass, cans, paper and cardboard, compost, general waste and a closed box for hazardous waste.

c4.title: A snorkelling trip from a villa in Negril
c4.text: A group of guests from a villa in Negril plan a snorkelling trip to a nearby reef. One guest, Mrs. Hall, puts on a lot of sunscreen on the boat just before she goes into the water. Another guest wants to feed the fish with bread. The tour boat's captain says he will drop his anchor next to the reef 'because it is quicker'. The villa's host, Mr. Reid, has been asked by the guests for advice.

c5.title: Lights on the beach at a Westmoreland villa
c5.text: A villa on a beach in Westmoreland has bright floodlights facing the sea. It is the turtle nesting season. In the morning, staff member Kevin sees tracks leading up the beach and an area of disturbed sand near the vegetation. The beach cleaner plans to rake the whole beach and then put the sun loungers out on the sand overnight.

questions.q: What should Tonya do about the running toilet in Villa 2?
o: Jiggle the handle for a few minutes and leave it if the water stops
Report it at once, with the room and the problem, so maintenance can fix it
Wait until check-out to see if the guests mention it to the front desk
Open the cistern and try to repair the valve herself with the tools in her trolley
questions.why: A running toilet wastes water all day and night, and it is worse in a drought. Housekeepers report faults promptly and do not try repairs they are not trained for.

questions.q: What is the best way to wash the vegetables in the kitchen?
o: In a filled basin, then use the rinse water on the plants
Under a gently running tap, so the dirt washes away more quickly
In a sink with the tap running slowly while the helper does other work
With the hose outside, so that the sink stays clean
questions.why: A filled basin uses much less water than a running tap, and plain vegetable rinse water is fine for plants. Running a tap while doing other work wastes water.

questions.q: Which is the best way to water the garden in this dry spell?
o: At midday with the hose, so that the plants are well watered for the hottest hours
At night with a sprinkler left running until morning
Every hour in small amounts through the day with a spray nozzle on the leaves
Early in the morning or late afternoon, at the roots, using tank or greywater
questions.why: Watering when it is cooler and at the roots means less is lost to evaporation, and using tank or treated greywater saves mains water. Midday and sprinklers waste water.

questions.q: The guest's card says that towels left on the floor will be changed, and towels hung up will be used again. What should Tonya do?
o: Change every towel in the room every day to be safe
Change only towels that look stained or wet
Change only the towels on the floor
Take all the towels away and put out new ones for the next day
questions.why: The towel reuse programme saves water, energy and detergent. Following the guest's choice, as the card says, respects the guest and saves resources.

questions.q: Which action best keeps the west-facing rooms cooler while using less electricity?
o: Open the windows and doors wide while the air conditioning is on
Set the air conditioning to its coldest temperature and leave it for the whole day
Draw the curtains at midday and use fans first
Leave the curtains open so that the room gets as much daylight as possible
questions.why: Keeping the sun out cuts the heat, and fans use much less electricity than air conditioning. Open windows with the AC on, and extra-cold settings, waste energy.

questions.q: What should Marcia do about the TV on standby and the charger in the empty room?
o: Leave them as they are, because standby uses no electricity
Switch them off at the wall socket and close the curtains
Leave them on in case the next guest wants the TV ready
Switch off the TV only and leave the charger plugged in
questions.why: Many appliances use power on standby, so they should be switched off at the socket when not needed. The charger may belong to the guest, so it is left in the room, not taken.

questions.q: How much energy will one 9 W LED bulb save compared with a 60 W bulb, for 5 hours' use in a day?
o: 2.55 kWh
0.3 kWh
questions.why: The 60 W bulb uses 0.06 kW × 5 h = 0.3 kWh. The 9 W LED uses 0.009 × 5 = 0.045 kWh. The saving is 0.3 − 0.045 = 0.255 kWh. 0.3 kWh is what the old bulb uses, and 0.045 kWh is the LED's use.

questions.q: What would the ten bulbs together save in a day?
o: 25.5 kWh
255 kWh
2.55 kWh
questions.why: 0.255 kWh saved per bulb × 10 bulbs = 2.55 kWh a day. Ten bulbs saving more than 25 kWh a day would be unlikely from such small bulbs.

questions.q: Where should the greasy pizza box go?
o: In the cardboard bin, because it is made of cardboard
In the compost bin, because it has food on it
In the hazardous waste box, because of the grease
In the general bin, as grease spoils recycling
questions.why: Food-soiled cardboard cannot be recycled, because grease and food contaminate the batch. It goes in the general waste. It is not hazardous waste.

questions.q: Which waste from the party is suitable for the compost heap?
o: The rinsed aluminium cans from the party table
The broken fluorescent tube from the terrace
The mango peelings and coffee grounds
The greasy pizza box that was left on the sand
questions.why: Fruit peelings and coffee grounds rot down into compost. Metal cans are recycled, the tube is hazardous waste, and the greasy box goes to general waste.

questions.q: How should the broken fluorescent tube be handled?
o: Put it in the glass recycling bin, because the tube is made of glass
Put it carefully in the hazardous waste box
Wrap it in newspaper and put it in the general bin
Bury it in the garden, away from the plants
questions.why: Fluorescent tubes contain mercury, which harms people and the environment. They go in the hazardous waste box and must not be put in glass recycling or general bins, or buried.

questions.q: What should Mr. Reid say about Mrs. Hall's sunscreen?
o: Use a mineral sunscreen, put on well before swimming
It does not matter what sunscreen she uses, because the sea washes it off
She should put on extra sunscreen just before she jumps in the water
She should not wear any sunscreen at all
questions.why: Some sunscreen ingredients are linked to coral damage. Mineral, reef-friendly products applied well before swimming, with a rash guard, protect both her skin and the reef.

questions.q: The guest wants to feed the fish bread. What is the best advice?
o: Do not feed the fish; it changes their behaviour
Bread is fine, but nothing else should be fed to the fish
It is fine if the fish come close enough for a good photo
It is fine if she throws only a few small pieces
questions.why: Feeding fish changes how they behave and can upset the reef's balance. Visitors should look but not feed.

questions.q: The captain wants to drop the anchor beside the reef. What should the villa do?
o: Let him anchor, as long as it is not directly on the coral
Tell the guests to jump off and swim ahead of him
Leave it to the guests to decide what to do
Ask him to use a mooring buoy instead
questions.why: An anchor and its chain can smash coral that took many years to grow. Mooring buoys let boats tie up without harm. The villa can choose operators who use them.

questions.q: Why should the guests not take coral or shells home?
o: They are likely to be fragile and break in the suitcase on the way home
They are heavy and may make the luggage cost extra at the airport
They are part of the reef and beach; removing them harms it
They may carry germs that could make guests ill on the flight home
questions.why: Coral and shells provide homes and protection and are part of the natural beach and reef. Taking them away damages the place visitors come to enjoy.

questions.q: Why should the floodlights facing the sea be switched off, shaded or turned down?
o: Lights bring too many insects onto the beach terrace at night
Hatchlings crawl towards the lights, not the sea
Lights make the water look darker to the guests on the terrace
Lights use electricity, which is expensive at night
questions.why: Baby turtles find the sea by its brightness, so lights on the beach send them the wrong way. Shielding lights protects them (and also saves energy).

questions.q: What should Kevin do about the tracks and disturbed sand?
o: Dig into the sand to see whether there are eggs
Leave it alone and report it to his supervisor
Rake the sand flat so that the beach looks neat
Move the tracks to another part of the beach
questions.why: Turtle nests are protected. Digging or raking could break the eggs. Staff mark the area if told to, keep people and equipment away and report it.

questions.q: What should be done with the sun loungers at night?
o: Put them away from the sand at night
Leave them on the sand so that they are ready in the morning
Line them up at the water's edge to show where the beach ends
Pile them on the area where the tracks end to protect it
questions.why: Loungers can block a female turtle coming up the beach to nest. Putting them away at night keeps the beach clear.

questions.q: The meter at a villa read 18 420 kWh last week and 18 605 kWh this week. If the villa pays J$60 per unit (an example rate only), what did the week's electricity cost?
questions.why: Units used = 18 605 − 18 420 = 185 kWh. Cost = 185 × 60 = J$11 100. The bigger figures come from multiplying the meter readings instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A villa in St. Elizabeth wants to cut food miles. Which tomatoes should the cook buy?
o: Tomatoes imported in a box from another country
Tomatoes bought from a supplier in another island
Tomatoes grown on a farm in the same parish
Tomatoes bought from a distant supplier because they are cheaper
questions.why: Food miles measure how far food travels. Buying from nearby farms means less fuel, less packaging and fresher produce, and supports the local community. Quality and safety must still be checked.
